div.head: 470. Memorandum of Conversation

list.label: SUBJECT
list.item: President Reagan’s Expanded Meeting with Venezuelan President Herrera Campins

list.label: U.S.
list.item: Assistant Secretary of State Thomas O. Enders

list.label: VENEZUELAN
list.item: Minister of the Presidency Garcia Bustillos

div.p: President Reagan briefly reviewed for the enlarged group what he and President Herrera had discussed in the Oval Office. The President then asked Secretary Haig what might be covered in this meeting. The Secretary said that Secretary Weinberger might wish to discuss the F–16’s. We should also touch on the residual petroleum nationalization issues and on the follow-up to Cancun. The Secretary said President Herrera might also have some matters to raise.

Secretary Weinberger said that the Reagan Administration has agreed to the sale of F–16’s to Venezuela, but for tactical reasons the proposal was not submitted to Congress until recently, so that this sale would not become confused with other arms sales problems. Now we believe that Congress will approve the sale. The Congress is, however, an independent body and one can never be certain. Secretary Weinberger said that we will make strong arguments and we are confident we will see it approved by Congress. We will also try to speed up delivery of some of the aircraft as much as possible.

President Reagan asked whether President Herrera would like to bring up other issues. President Herrera said that there are three main issues, aside from bilateral questions between our two governments, that he believes should be discussed during his visit to Washington:
— First is the concrete and rapid implementation of the discussions of the four nations at the Nassau Meeting.
— Second is an effective search for a democratic way out in Salvador.
— And third is the follow-up to Cancun on global negotiations.

These three issues relate to the support for democracy in the world. The first two relate directly to democracy. If we can be successful we will achieve a worldwide blow against Communism. On the follow-up to Cancun, democracies should come up with some proposals that will demonstrate that democracies are more creative and more able than other systems to deal with the changing world. He said that these three topics can be discussed at later meetings. President Herrera thanked Secretary Weinberger for his comments on the F–16.
President Reagan concluded the meeting by saying that in the Wednesday meeting the two Presidents should discuss Cancun and bilateral issues.

note.p: Source: Reagan Library, Executive Secretariat, NSC Subject File, Memorandums of Conversation—President Reagan (11/19/1981–11/27/1981). Secret. Drafted on November 19 by Luers; cleared in S/S and the NSC. The meeting took place in the Cabinet Room.

In telegram 10293 from Caracas, October 30, the Embassy provided suggested topics to raise during Herrera’s visit. Regarding the petroleum nationalization claims the Embassy wrote: “We hope the President will bring this issue directly to Herrera’s attention. He might point out that it unfortunately represents a potential sore point in the otherwise excellent relations between our two countries. We feel strongly that justice needs to be done. Moreover, we fear that failure soon to come to an equitable settlement could damage Venezuela’s international reputation and standing with the world’s lending agencies.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D810515–0034)
